before.exam_tip_html: For the 4-mark Explain question, examiners want a chain of reasoning, not a list. State the cause, then the process, then the result. For example: ‘Air rises at the equator (cause) because it is heated by direct sunlight, expands and becomes less dense (process). It cools at altitude, condensing water vapour, which releases heavy rainfall over equatorial regions (result).’ The 3 SPaG marks per paper reward precise terms like Hadley cell, Coriolis and prevailing wind — use them.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Hadley cell?
A) A loop of moving air between 30° and 60° latitude
B) A loop of moving air between the equator and 30° latitude
C) A current of warm water in the Atlantic Ocean
D) A weather front that brings rain to the UK
practice_questions.marks: B) A loop of moving air between the equator and 30° latitude. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'atmospheric pressure'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The weight or force of air pressing down on the Earth's surface, measured in millibars or hectopascals.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'The weight of air pressing on the surface.' [1 mark]
Developing/Emerging: vague reference to weather or temperature without naming weight or air column. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of high-pressure and low-pressure zones.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Low pressure at the equator (rising air, heavy rainfall, equatorial belt of forests).
• High pressure at around 30°N and 30°S (sinking air, location of major deserts).
• Low pressure again at 60° latitude (rising air, temperate rainfall belt).
• High pressure over the poles (sinking cold dry air).
Mastering: clearly described locations of all three pressure types. [3]
Secure: two correctly described. [2]
Developing: one correct point. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how global atmospheric circulation creates the world's great deserts.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Air rises at the equator, having been heated by intense sunlight (point 1).
• At altitude it cools, releasing moisture as rainfall, then travels polewards.
• At around 30° latitude this dry air sinks back to the surface (point 2).
• Sinking air warms by compression, can hold more moisture, so very little rainfall reaches the surface — creating arid zones such as the Sahara, Arabian and Atacama deserts.
Mastering: full chain of reasoning linking sinking air → high pressure → aridity → named desert. [4]
Secure: cause–effect chain identifying sinking air and dry conditions. [3]
Developing: identifies sinking air at 30° but no full chain. [2]
Emerging: simple statement that 30° is dry. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A climate graph shows monthly rainfall in a tropical location: 200, 220, 210, 195, 205, 215, 225, 230, 220, 215, 210, 200 (mm).
Calculate the mean monthly rainfall. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: total = 2,545 mm; mean = 2,545 ÷ 12 = 212.08 mm (accept 212.1 or 212). Working shown. [4]
Secure: correct method and correct arithmetic to 211–213 with units. [3]
Developing: correct method but arithmetic error of <±5 mm or units missing. [2]
Emerging: attempts addition or division but does not complete or shows working error. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine how global atmospheric circulation influences the location of biomes around the world.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tropical rainforests cluster on the equator because rising Hadley-cell air produces year-round heavy rainfall, ideal for dense vegetation.
• Deserts cluster at ~30° latitude because Hadley-cell air sinks, creating high pressure and aridity (Sahara, Arabian, Australian).
• Temperate biomes occur at 50–60° latitude where the Ferrel cell rises, generating regular but moderate rainfall (UK deciduous forest, grassland).
• Polar biomes (tundra) lie under the Polar cell where cold sinking air gives very low precipitation and freezing temperatures.
• Ocean currents modify biomes locally — e.g. North Atlantic Drift gives north-west Europe temperate climate further north than expected.
Mastering (7–8): sustained, well-evidenced argument linking circulation to multiple biomes with specific examples and clear chains of reasoning.
Secure (5–6): clear argument and at least two named biomes linked to circulation cells.
Developing (3–4): basic links between cells and rainfall, limited examples.
Emerging (1–2): simple statements without explanation.

before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Extended Writing question, structure your answer around two or three big points, each developed with reasoning AND a specific named example. Generic statements like ‘humans pollute’ will not score — examiners want CO₂ ppm rises, named feedback loops, named places affected. Always link causes to consequences. The 4 SPaG marks reward terms like enhanced greenhouse effect, Milankovitch cycles and permafrost.

before.content_html:
Storms of Extraordinary Power

A tropical cyclone is the most powerful storm on Earth. Called hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the western Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean, they are all the same phenomenon. They can be 800 km wide, last for weeks, and pack winds over 250 km/h. They form, strengthen and dissipate in patterns geographers can predict — but every cyclone is a unique threat to the people in its path.

Where and Why They Form

Tropical cyclones need a specific recipe: ocean water above 26.5°C, depths of at least 50 m of warm water, atmospheric instability, low wind shear (wind speed similar at different altitudes), and being at least 5° latitude away from the equator (so the Coriolis effect can spin them up). These conditions occur in summer and autumn over the warmest tropical seas: Atlantic hurricanes (June–November), Pacific typhoons (May–November) and Indian Ocean cyclones (April–December). They form in the rising arm of the Hadley cell where warm, moist air is already lifting; tracks curve westwards under the trade winds, then poleward.

Key Fact

Tropical cyclones need warm ocean (26.5°C+), atmospheric instability, low wind shear and the Coriolis effect. They cannot form on the equator and they die over land or cooler water.

Anatomy of a Cyclone

Warm, moist air rises rapidly at the storm centre, condensing into towering clouds and releasing huge amounts of energy as latent heat — this is the cyclone’s ‘fuel’. Air spirals inwards along the surface, deflected by the Coriolis effect into a rotation. Pressure at the centre drops far below normal. The eye is the calm centre — clear skies, no wind — while the eye-wall just outside it is where the most violent winds and heaviest rain are concentrated. Spiral rain bands stretch outwards for hundreds of kilometres.

The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies hurricanes by sustained wind speed: Category 1 (119–153 km/h, some damage), Category 3 (178–208 km/h, devastating), Category 5 (over 252 km/h, catastrophic). The scale focuses on wind, but storm-surge flooding often kills more people than wind alone.

The Hazards They Bring

Cyclones cause damage in three main ways. High winds tear off roofs, snap trees, hurl debris and disable power lines. Intense rainfall — often 200–500 mm in a single day — causes flash flooding and triggers landslides on steep slopes. The storm surge is the most deadly: a sudden rise in sea level, often 4–9 m, that can drown coastal communities. Hurricane Katrina’s 8.5 m surge in 2005 destroyed New Orleans levees and caused most of the storm’s 1,800 deaths.

Key Fact

The three primary hazards of a tropical cyclone are high winds, intense rainfall and storm surge. Storm surge usually causes the most deaths because of widespread coastal flooding.

Why Vulnerability Varies

Two countries can be hit by similar storms but suffer hugely different outcomes. Vulnerability depends on three factors. Physical: low-lying coasts (Bangladesh, Pacific islands) and densely populated coastal cities (Manila, Miami) are at greater risk. Social: poverty forces some communities into flimsy housing or risky locations; warning systems may not reach the most isolated; some have less education about evacuation. Economic: developed countries can build sea walls, fund early-warning systems and rebuild quickly; developing countries cannot. The 2008 Cyclone Nargis killed an estimated 138,000 people in Myanmar — partly because the military government delayed international aid.

In a developed country like the USA, cyclone preparedness includes weather satellites, hurricane hunters (aircraft), the National Hurricane Center, evacuation orders, building codes (Florida) and federal disaster funding through FEMA. In a developing country like the Philippines, response often relies on overseas aid, less robust building stock and weaker pre-disaster planning — though the Philippines has improved markedly since Typhoon Haiyan (2013, 6,300+ deaths) by setting up faster evacuation and hardened shelters.

Preparation and Response

Effective preparation involves four layers. Forecasting uses weather satellites to track cyclones days before landfall. Warnings are issued through TV, radio, mobile alerts and sirens. Evacuation moves residents to inland shelters; coastal cities like Tampa rehearse evacuation routes. Defences include sea-walls, surge barriers and storm-resistant building codes. The Netherlands and Bangladesh have both invested heavily in surge defences. Bangladesh’s coastal cyclone-shelter network has cut deaths from over 300,000 (1970 cyclone) to under 5,000 (similar 2007 storm).
before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Examine question on cyclone responses, always compare a developed country (e.g. USA Hurricane Katrina or Florida response) with a developing or emerging country (e.g. Philippines Typhoon Haiyan or Bangladesh). Examiners want named cases, specific death tolls, specific dollar costs — not just ‘richer countries respond better’. Contrast preparation, response and recovery stages. The 4 SPaG marks reward terms like storm surge, Saffir-Simpson and vulnerability.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT needed for a tropical cyclone to form?
A) Sea surface temperature above 26.5°C
B) Position at least 5° from the equator
C) Cold polar air mass colliding with warm tropical air
D) Low atmospheric wind shear
practice_questions.marks: C) Cold polar air mass colliding with warm tropical air. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'storm surge'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A wall of seawater pushed onto the coast by a tropical cyclone's low pressure and strong onshore winds.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Sea level rising suddenly because of a storm.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of tropical cyclone tracks.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Form between roughly 5°–25° latitude in summer/autumn over warm tropical oceans (Atlantic, W. Pacific, Indian Ocean).
• Move westwards under the trade winds, then curve polewards.
• Decay over land or over cooler water (above 30° latitude).
Mastering: pattern with latitude band and curved tracks. [3]
Secure: identifies tropical formation and one feature of track. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain why some countries are more vulnerable to tropical cyclones than others.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Physical: low-lying densely populated coasts (Bangladesh delta, Pacific atolls) flood easily; mountainous islands suffer landslides.
• Social: poorer communities live in flimsy housing or informal settlements with no protection; warnings reach remote villages later.
• Economic: developing countries cannot afford sea walls, satellites or robust building codes; recovery depends on aid.
Mastering: linked physical, social AND economic factors with examples. [4]
Secure: two factors developed. [3]
Developing: identifies one factor. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Hurricane Katrina caused 1,800 deaths and Cyclone Nargis caused 138,000 deaths.
Calculate how many times more deaths Cyclone Nargis caused than Hurricane Katrina. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 138,000 ÷ 1,800 = 76.67 times (accept 76–77). Working clear. [4]
Secure: 76 or 77 with method shown. [3]
Developing: division attempted but arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: tries subtraction or wrong operation. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the effectiveness of methods used to prepare for and respond to tropical cyclones in a developed country and in a developing or emerging country.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Developed country (USA, Hurricane Sandy 2012 or Florida): satellite tracking via the National Hurricane Center, mandatory evacuation orders, federal disaster funding through FEMA, building codes that require storm-resistant construction. Effectiveness: deaths often kept low (Sandy ~233 in USA), but rebuilding costs huge ($70 bn).
• Developing/emerging country (Bangladesh, since 1970): cyclone shelter network of over 12,000 raised concrete buildings, mass evacuation drills, mobile-phone warnings. Death tolls have fallen from over 300,000 (1970) to under 5,000 in similar storms.
• Differences: developed countries have wealth and technology but coastal property is concentrated and very high-value; developing countries have built community-based systems out of necessity, sometimes with better mortality outcomes.
• Limits: even rich countries fail (Katrina 2005, levees gave way); even prepared developing nations face climate change increasing storm frequency.
Mastering (7–8): nuanced comparison naming cases on both sides with effectiveness measures.
Secure (5–6): clear examples of each, comparison of two methods.
Developing (3–4): basic comparison without specifics.
Emerging (1–2): generalisations without examples.

before.content_html:
A Restless Planet

Beneath our feet, the Earth is hot and moving. The surface is broken into giant slabs of rock called tectonic plates. Where these plates meet, volcanic eruptions and earthquakes shake the surface. Understanding why — and where they happen — helps geographers predict, prepare and reduce risk for the billions of people who live near plate boundaries.

Inside the Earth

The Earth has four main layers. The inner core is solid iron and nickel at around 6,000°C. The outer core is liquid iron and nickel; circulating currents here generate Earth’s magnetic field. The mantle is hot, slow-flowing rock about 2,900 km thick; its upper part — the asthenosphere — is partially molten and acts like very thick treacle. The crust is the thin (5–70 km) outermost layer; its rigid uppermost part plus the very top of the mantle together form the lithosphere — the ‘plates’ themselves.

Key Fact

Heat from the core (released by the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium) drives convection currents in the mantle. These currents drag the lithospheric plates around at 2–10 cm per year — about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Three Types of Plate Boundary

Plates meet at three kinds of boundary. At a convergent boundary, plates collide. If oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser oceanic plate is forced down (subducted) into the mantle, melting and rising as andesitic magma to form explosive volcanoes such as those in the Andes and Cascade Range. The Pacific ‘Ring of Fire’ is a chain of these convergent boundaries.

At a divergent boundary, plates pull apart. Magma rises into the gap and cools to form new oceanic crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs the length of the Atlantic; Iceland sits directly on it, with frequent fissure-style basaltic eruptions. At a conservative boundary, plates slide past each other. There is no volcanic activity, but stress builds and releases as earthquakes — the San Andreas Fault between the Pacific and North American plates is the classic example.

A few volcanoes sit far from any plate boundary. They form over hotspots — isolated plumes of hot mantle rising through the lithosphere. The Hawaiian Islands sit on the moving Pacific plate above a fixed hotspot; over millions of years, a chain of volcanic islands forms as the plate drifts north-westwards. Yellowstone is another hotspot, sitting under the centre of the North American plate.

Volcanic and Earthquake Hazards

Volcanic hazards depend on magma type. Basaltic magma (Hawaii, Iceland) is fluid and erupts as gentle lava flows; loss of life is rare though property damage can be huge. Andesitic and rhyolitic magma (Andes, Pacific Ring) is sticky; gas builds up and eruptions are explosive. Hazards include lava flows, ash falls (which collapse roofs and ground aircraft), pyroclastic flows (super-heated gas and ash travelling at 700 km/h), lahars (volcanic mudflows when heat melts ice or rain mixes with ash) and toxic gases. Mount St Helens (1980) and Mount Pinatubo (1991) showed how lethal explosive eruptions can be.

Key Fact

Earthquake magnitude is measured on the moment magnitude scale (Mw): each whole-number step represents about 32× more energy. A magnitude 7 quake releases roughly 1,000× the energy of a magnitude 5.

Earthquakes and Tsunami

Earthquakes happen when stored stress along a fault is released as seismic waves. Shallow quakes (under 70 km deep) are usually the most damaging because the energy reaches the surface concentrated. The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake off Japan was a magnitude 9.0–9.1 megathrust quake at a convergent boundary — one of the largest ever recorded. It triggered a tsunami with waves up to 40 m high that killed around 18,000 people and destroyed the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.

Why Impacts Vary

A magnitude 7 quake in Haiti (2010) killed an estimated 230,000. A magnitude 6.9 quake in Christchurch, New Zealand (2011) killed 185. The hazard was similar; the vulnerability was not. Wealth, building codes, public education, emergency planning and political stability shape outcomes far more than magnitude alone. Developed countries can prepare; developing countries often must rely on overseas aid for short-term relief and long-term reconstruction.

Japan’s response to the 2011 Tōhoku quake combined strict building codes, automatic train shutdowns, sea walls (some of which were overtopped), drilled school children and a Self-Defence Force ready to respond — yet still suffered 18,000 deaths because of the unprecedented tsunami. Haiti’s 2010 response was hampered by collapsed government buildings, no enforced building codes, and an over-reliance on a single airport. The contrast is not perfect but illustrates how preparation reduces — though never eliminates — tectonic risk.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Examine question on tectonic hazards, you must compare a developed country with a developing or emerging country. Pick contrasting examples (Japan 2011 vs Haiti 2010 is a strong pairing) and use specific death tolls and dollar costs. Examiners reward primary vs secondary impact distinctions: primary impacts are immediate (collapsed buildings, deaths from shaking); secondary impacts are knock-on (tsunami, fires, disease outbreaks, economic disruption).

before.content_html:
What Does ‘Development’ Mean?

Development is the process by which a country improves the economic, social and political wellbeing of its people. It used to be measured almost entirely by income, but today geographers recognise that wealth alone misses important things. A country can have rising income while inequality, poor health or a lack of political freedom limit how that wealth helps ordinary people.

Single-Indicator Measures

The classic economic measure is GDP per capita. It is easy to compare and updated yearly. The World Bank classifies countries as low income (under $1,135 per year), lower-middle, upper-middle, or high income (over $13,845). But GDP per capita has weaknesses: it ignores how income is distributed, hides the informal economy (street trading, subsistence farming), and says nothing about quality of life.

Other single indicators include literacy rate (% of adults who can read and write), life expectancy (average years a newborn is expected to live) and infant mortality rate (deaths per 1,000 live births in the first year). These tell different stories: Cuba has GDP per capita roughly a tenth of the UK’s but life expectancy almost the same, because of strong public health.

Key Fact

Single-indicator measures (GDP per capita, life expectancy, literacy rate) are useful for quick comparisons but each captures only one dimension of development. They can disagree sharply about how ‘developed’ a country is.

Composite Measures: HDI

The Human Development Index was created by the UN in 1990. It combines three measures: GDP per capita (income), mean and expected years of schooling (education), and life expectancy (health). The result is a single number from 0 to 1. Norway typically tops the index (0.96), the UK is around 0.94, while many sub-Saharan African countries score below 0.5. HDI better captures development than GDP alone, but it still ignores inequality, environmental degradation and political freedom.

The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale of 0 (everyone earns the same) to 1 (one person earns everything). The Nordic countries score around 0.25, the UK around 0.35 and South Africa around 0.63 — one of the most unequal societies on Earth. Two countries with the same GDP per capita can have very different living conditions if Gini differs sharply. Examiners reward students who pair GDP with Gini in their answers.

Demographic Indicators

A country’s demographic data tells a story too. Fertility rate (births per woman) is around 1.6 in the UK and 4.5 in Niger. Death rate falls as healthcare improves. Population structure (drawn as a population pyramid) shifts from a wide-base ‘triangle’ in low-development countries (many young children, few elderly) to a ‘column’ in highly developed countries (an ageing population). Maternal and infant mortality rates fall sharply with development — from over 500 deaths per 100,000 births in the lowest-developed countries to around 5–10 in the highest.

Key Fact

Three categories: developing countries (low GDP per capita, high fertility, low life expectancy — e.g. Niger, Bangladesh), emerging (rapid economic growth, falling fertility — e.g. India, Brazil), developed (high GDP, low fertility, ageing population — e.g. UK, Japan).

Theories of Why Development Differs

Two contrasting theories try to explain why development varies. Rostow’s modernisation theory (1960) argues that countries pass through five stages: traditional society (subsistence farming); preconditions for take-off (commercial farming, infrastructure); take-off (rapid growth in key industries); drive to maturity (technology spreads); high mass consumption (rich service-led economy). Investment, education and globalisation help countries climb the ladder. The UK and South Korea are examples of countries that have moved through all five stages.

Frank’s dependency theory (1967) argues the opposite: rich countries (the ‘core’) actively keep poor countries (the ‘periphery’) underdeveloped through unequal trade, foreign debt and the legacy of colonialism. The core extracts cheap raw materials and sells back expensive manufactured goods. The periphery becomes locked into supplying primary commodities. Real-world development is messy: South Korea broke dependency, but Frank’s theory still explains many post-colonial economies.

Global inequality has many causes. Historical: colonial powers extracted resources and left ex-colonies with weak institutions; environmental: tropical climates can hamper agriculture; landlocked countries struggle to trade. Economic: terms of trade often favour exporters of manufactured goods over raw commodity exporters. Political: corruption, conflict and weak rule of law deter investment. Social: poor health and education hold back productivity. No country’s development is shaped by just one factor.

flashcard_questions.a: The process by which a country improves the economic, social and political wellbeing of its people.
The total value of goods and services produced in a country, divided by its population.
flashcard_questions.q: What does GDP per capita measure?
What is one weakness of GDP per capita as a development measure?

flashcard_questions.a: The Human Development Index, a composite of income, education and life expectancy on a 0-1 scale.
Around 0.96 — typically the highest in the world.
Income inequality within a country, on a scale of 0 to 1.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the Gini coefficient measure?

flashcard_questions.a: Countries pass through five stages of growth from traditional society to high mass consumption.
Rich 'core' countries keep poor 'periphery' countries underdeveloped through unequal trade and the legacy of colonialism.
Wide base and narrow top — a triangle, showing many young people and few elderly.
flashcard_questions.q: What shape is the population pyramid of a developing country?

flashcard_questions.a: Narrower base and wider middle — a column, showing low birth rate and an ageing population.
flashcard_questions.q: What shape is the population pyramid of a developed country?

flashcard_questions.a: They face higher costs to trade because they depend on neighbours for sea access.
flashcard_questions.q: Why do landlocked countries often have lower development?

flashcard_questions.a: Around 4.5 children per woman — among the highest in the world.
flashcard_questions.q: Roughly what is Niger's fertility rate?

before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Examine question on development approaches, examiners reward students who balance top-down AND bottom-up examples. Always name specific projects (Three Gorges Dam vs Practical Action solar-irrigation), specific organisations (World Bank, Oxfam, Apple) and specific outcomes (number of people lifted out of poverty, displacement totals, economic growth percentages). Avoid generic statements like ‘rich countries help poor ones’.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of bottom-up, intermediate-technology development?
A) China's Three Gorges Dam
B) A solar-lantern programme run by an NGO in rural Kenya
C) A motorway built by a national government
D) A new international airport
practice_questions.marks: B) A solar-lantern programme run by an NGO in rural Kenya. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'transnational corporation (TNC)'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A company that operates in two or more countries, with offices, factories or shops in multiple nations.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A big company that works in lots of countries.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of intermediate technology.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Low cost — affordable for poor communities.
• Locally repairable — communities can maintain it without specialists.
• Suited to existing skill levels and resources of the population.
• Sustainable — uses renewable energy or local materials.
Mastering: two characteristics with explanation. [3]
Secure: two characteristics named. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how TNCs can both help and harm a developing country.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Help: bring foreign direct investment, create jobs, transfer skills and technology, raise tax revenues, push up wages over time.
• Harm: profits often returned home not reinvested locally; can pay low wages or use poor working conditions; multiple-country accounting can avoid corporation tax; environmental harm in countries with weak regulation.
• Specific: Apple manufacturing in China lifted Foxconn workers' wages but came under criticism for working hours and environment.
Mastering: balanced 'help and harm' with named example. [4]

practice_questions.text: A new TNC factory in Vietnam pays 200 workers $300/month each. How much extra wage income enters the local economy each year? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: monthly = 200 × $300 = $60,000; annual = $60,000 × 12 = $720,000. Working clear and units stated. [4]
Secure: $720,000 with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error, method correct. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the advantages and disadvantages of top-down and bottom-up approaches to development.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Top-down advantages: scale (Three Gorges Dam now provides 22.5 GW of electricity to China); speed (large infrastructure built in years not decades); national-level economic growth.
• Top-down disadvantages: cost (Three Gorges cost over $40 bn, much from World Bank loans creating debt); displacement (1.3 million people relocated); environmental damage (loss of habitats, sediment build-up).
• Bottom-up advantages: appropriate to need (Practical Action solar-drip irrigation in Zimbabwe doubled smallholder yields cheaply); locally owned and sustainable; few people displaced.
• Bottom-up disadvantages: small scale (cannot replace a national grid); patchy funding from charity; cannot deliver national infrastructure.
• Conclusion: real development needs both — large infrastructure for grids, ports and rail; community-scale work for clean water, agriculture and health.
Mastering (7–8): both approaches with strengths AND weaknesses, named examples.
Secure (5–6): both approaches with examples, less balance.
Developing (3–4): one approach in detail.
Emerging (1–2): vague.

lessons.title: Case Study: Development in an Emerging Country (India)

before.content_html:
An Emerging Powerhouse

In 1991, India faced a financial crisis with only enough foreign currency to pay for two weeks of imports. The government chose to open the economy: cutting tariffs, welcoming foreign investment, dismantling old controls. Three decades on, India is the world’s fifth-largest economy, with over 1.4 billion people. It is a classic emerging country — but the growth has been uneven. This case study explains how India got here and what comes next.

Site, Situation and Context

India’s site — what is found at the location — covers 3.3 million km² of South Asia, with the Himalayas in the north, the Thar Desert in the west, and a vast tropical and subtropical interior. Its situation — how it relates to other places — is favourable for trade: long coastlines on the Indian Ocean, ports at Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai, and proximity to the Persian Gulf, Southeast Asia and East Africa. Connectivity has improved with new airports, mobile networks reaching 95% of the country, and a fibre-optic backbone supporting the IT industry.

Politically, India is the world’s largest democracy, with a federal structure of 28 states. Its formal Independence from Britain in 1947 left it with English-speaking elites, a robust legal system, and an inherited rail network — all useful for trade and global business. Culturally, the country has 22 official languages and immense diversity. Hinduism is the majority religion, but India is also home to large Muslim, Christian, Sikh, Buddhist and Jain populations.

Key Fact

India: population 1.4 billion (2024); 5th-largest economy by GDP, 3rd by purchasing power; over 22 official languages; economic liberalisation began in 1991; megacities include Mumbai (financial), Delhi (political), Bengaluru (IT) and Kolkata (cultural-historical).

Globalisation Drives Growth

Since 1991, India’s economy has been transformed by globalisation. Average GDP growth between 2003 and 2018 was around 7% per year — second only to China among major economies. The composition of the economy has shifted dramatically. In 1990, agriculture employed about 60% of workers and produced 30% of GDP. Today agriculture is around 18% of GDP, services 50%, and industry 25%. The IT and business-services sector centred on Bengaluru exports software and back-office work to the world — Wipro, Infosys and TCS rival US tech companies.

India received around $84 bn of foreign direct investment in 2022 — up from less than $1 bn in 1990. The largest sources are Singapore, the USA, Mauritius and Japan. Investment flows into IT services, telecommunications, manufacturing (Apple now assembles iPhones in Tamil Nadu), pharmaceuticals and renewable energy. The government’s ‘Make in India’ programme since 2014 has actively courted manufacturing FDI to reduce dependence on imports and create jobs for the 12 million young Indians entering the workforce each year.

Demographic and Social Change

Rapid economic change has reshaped Indian society. The fertility rate has fallen from 5.4 in 1960 to 2.0 today, just below replacement. Life expectancy has risen from 41 years (1960) to 70. Around 35% of Indians now live in urban areas, up from 17% in 1950. Tens of millions are leaving farms for cities — the rural-urban migration typical of emerging economies. New regions have emerged: Bengaluru’s IT corridor, Mumbai’s financial district, Gujarat’s industrial belt — the country’s ‘core’. Other regions, especially in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, lag behind — the ‘periphery’.

Key Fact

Around 415 million Indians escaped poverty between 2005 and 2021 (UN figures). But around 230 million still live on under $3.65 a day, and Delhi’s air pollution is among the worst in the world — a sign that growth has come at significant environmental cost.

Costs and Benefits

Benefits include rising living standards, falling extreme poverty, expansion of the middle class to around 350 million people, world-class IT companies, and improving infrastructure. Costs are real too: environmental damage — air and water pollution, especially in Delhi (PM2.5 levels routinely 10× WHO guidelines); inequality — women earn around 35% less than men, and the wealthiest 10% take more than 57% of national income; rising land and property prices; loss of farmland to urban sprawl. Globalisation has not benefited everyone equally.

India’s rapid core-periphery inequality growth has changed its position in the world. It is part of BRICS (alongside Brazil, Russia, China, South Africa) and the G20. It now leads the Quad security partnership with the USA, Japan and Australia. Its space programme reached the moon in 2023. India is no longer just a recipient of foreign aid — it now provides aid to smaller neighbours like Sri Lanka and Bhutan. But strained relations with neighbouring China (over disputed Himalayan borders) and Pakistan still shape regional politics.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Examine question on a case study, examiners reward depth over breadth. Use specific Indian figures throughout: GDP growth 7% per year, FDI of $84 bn in 2022, urban population 35%, fertility rate 2.0. Always link cause to consequence (e.g. liberalisation 1991 → FDI inflows → IT sector growth → middle class expansion). Generic answers about ‘emerging countries’ will not score the top band.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the largest sector of India's economy today?
A) Agriculture
B) Manufacturing
C) Services
D) Mining
practice_questions.marks: C) Services. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why India is a favourable location for foreign direct investment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: large English-speaking workforce; coastal access via Indian Ocean ports; large domestic market (1.4 bn people); 1991 liberalisation policies; 'Make in India' incentives; democratic government; growing middle class. [2 marks]
Secure: one reason. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the changing structure of India's economy since 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Decline of agriculture as a share of GDP from ~30% (1990) to ~18% (today).
• Rise of services from a smaller share to ~50% of GDP, dominated by IT and business services.
• Industry around 25%, with manufacturing growing through 'Make in India'.
Mastering: figures and trend across all three sectors. [3]
Secure: shift between two sectors with rough figures. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how globalisation has driven India's economic development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1991 liberalisation reduced tariffs and welcomed FDI, attracting TNCs that brought capital, skills and technology.
• Cheap mobile and internet connectivity, plus an English-speaking workforce, allowed India to become the world's back-office and software services hub (Bengaluru, Hyderabad).
• TNCs like Apple now manufacture in India (Tamil Nadu) for export; Infosys and TCS sell IT services to global clients.
• Result: GDP growth of ~7% per year, lifting 415 million people out of poverty.
Mastering: causal chain liberalisation → FDI → sector growth → poverty reduction. [4]

practice_questions.text:
If India's GDP grew at an average of 7% per year for 10 years, by what factor has it grown?
(Use the formula 1.07¹⁰ ≈ 1.97). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 1.07¹⁰ ≈ 1.97, so GDP nearly doubled (~97% increase). Working clear. [4]
Secure: states ~2× or 97% with method. [3]
Developing: ~70% (using simple addition not compounding) — partial credit for method. [2]
Emerging: any plausible attempt. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the positive and negative impacts of rapid economic development on people and the environment in India.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Positive — people: ~415 million lifted out of poverty since 2005; middle class now ~350 million; life expectancy up from 41 (1960) to 70; literacy rates rising; women's workforce participation expanding.
• Positive — environment: rapid expansion of solar power (160 GW capacity 2024); 'Clean India' (Swachh Bharat) sanitation programme; international climate pledges.
• Negative — people: inequality (top 10% take 57% of income); 230 million still in poverty; sharp regional gaps between Mumbai/Bengaluru core and Bihar/UP periphery; informal-sector workers without protection.
• Negative — environment: Delhi PM2.5 routinely 10× WHO limits; Yamuna and Ganges heavily polluted; loss of farmland to sprawl; coal still 70% of electricity.
• Conclusion: Growth has lifted hundreds of millions but at significant cost — sustainability remains a challenge.
Mastering (7–8): four named impacts (2 + 2) with figures.
Secure (5–6): three impacts with examples.
Developing (3–4): general statements, weak figures.
Emerging (1–2): one-sided.

before.content_html:
A Planet of City Dwellers

In 1950, only about 30% of people lived in towns and cities. By 2007 the world crossed a tipping point — for the first time in history, more than half of humanity was urban. Today the figure is around 57%, and the United Nations projects it will reach 68% by 2050. The next thirty years are expected to add more than 2 billion city dwellers, almost all of them in Asia and Africa. Urbanisation is one of the defining processes of our time, reshaping where people live, how they work and the pressures placed on the environment.

Why Are Cities Growing?

Two processes drive urban growth. The first is rural-urban migration — people moving from villages to cities. The second is natural increase, where the urban population grows because births outnumber deaths inside the city itself. Migrants are typically young adults of working age, so once they arrive they have children, accelerating growth further.

People move because of push factors in the countryside and pull factors in cities. Common push factors include rural poverty, mechanisation of farming reducing labour needs, drought or land degradation, and limited access to schools or hospitals. Pull factors include better-paid jobs in factories or services, brighter-lit streets and entertainment, the chance of a university education and access to clean water and electricity. The reality often falls short of the hope — many migrants end up in informal slums — but the contrast with rural conditions still makes the move worthwhile.

Key Fact

The world urban share rose from about 30% (1950) to roughly 57% (today) and is projected to hit 68% by 2050. Almost all future urban growth will happen in developing and emerging countries.

Different Speeds in Different Places

Not every country is urbanising at the same speed. Developed countries are already 80% or more urban; their growth is now slow or even slightly negative as people retire to the coast or countryside. Emerging countries like India and Brazil are urbanising fast as factories, services and infrastructure expand. Developing countries have the lowest urban share but the highest rates of urban growth. Africa is the most rural continent today but is urbanising the quickest — Lagos in Nigeria adds about 77 new residents every hour.

Cities also reshape themselves internally. Suburbanisation is the spread of housing outwards into the urban-rural fringe, common across the UK from the 1930s. Counter-urbanisation is people moving from cities to small towns or villages, which has happened in parts of southern England as remote working has spread. Re-urbanisation is the return of people to inner-city areas after regeneration — London Docklands, Manchester city centre and Liverpool waterfront are British examples. Most cities show all three processes happening at once in different neighbourhoods.

Megacities and Urban Primacy

A megacity has more than 10 million inhabitants. In 1950 there were only two: New York and Tokyo. By 2025 there are around 35, and the great majority are in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Tokyo (about 37 million) and Delhi (about 33 million) lead the league. Most growth in the next twenty years will come from cities like Lagos, Dhaka, Karachi and Kinshasa — cities most British students would struggle to place on a map.

In many countries one city stands far above the rest in size, wealth and political importance. Geographers call this urban primacy. Bangkok dwarfs every other Thai city. Lima houses about a third of all Peruvians. Lagos handles most of Nigeria’s formal economy. Primacy concentrates investment but also concentrates problems — traffic, pollution, slum housing — into a single overcrowded centre.

Key Fact

A megacity has over 10 million people. Numbers grew from 2 megacities (1950) to roughly 35 today, with most new megacities forming in Asia and Africa. Urban primacy is when one city dominates a country.

Formal vs Informal Economies

Cities in different parts of the world have different economies. The formal sector includes registered factories, offices and retail. The informal sector covers street trading, recycling, casual labour and home-based work. In developed countries the informal sector is small. In emerging cities like Mumbai or Lagos it employs over half the workforce. Conditions are often poor, with no contracts, sick pay or pensions, but the sector absorbs new arrivals who cannot find formal jobs immediately.

To find percentage change in urban population: subtract the start value from the end value, divide by the start value and multiply by 100. For example, Lagos grew from about 7.3 million in 2000 to 15.4 million in 2024. Change = 8.1 million; 8.1 / 7.3 = 1.11; × 100 = 111% growth in 24 years. Annual rate ≈ 111 / 24 ≈ 4.6% a year. Examiner tip: always show the working, even if the final figure is wrong — method marks are awarded.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark megacity case-study question, examiners expect specific named places (Dharavi, Nariman Point, Antilia, Navi Mumbai), specific numbers (22 million people, 6% of GDP, 41% in slums) and a clear structure: site/situation, growth, opportunities AND challenges. Don’t answer with generic ‘developing world city’ points — mark schemes reward specifics. Practise drawing a labelled sketch of Mumbai with CBD, Dharavi, Bandra and the airports.
before.content_html:
Mumbai: India’s Economic Capital

Mumbai sits on the west coast of India, on a long thin peninsula stretching into the Arabian Sea. Its population is around 22 million in the wider metropolitan area, making it one of the world’s ten largest cities. Mumbai is the financial heart of India: it hosts the Bombay Stock Exchange, the Reserve Bank of India and Bollywood, the world’s biggest film industry by output. Roughly 6% of India’s GDP is generated within Greater Mumbai — despite the city covering less than 0.1% of the country’s land area.

Site, Situation and Connectivity

Mumbai’s site is unusual: the city was originally seven small islands, joined together over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries by land reclamation. Its situation is exceptional. The deep natural harbour faces the Indian Ocean and gave the British East India Company a base from which to trade with Africa, Arabia and Europe. Mumbai is now India’s busiest container port and home to its largest international airport. Mumbai’s connectivity includes 1,400 km of suburban rail (the world’s busiest commuter system), national highways, and undersea data cables connecting India to global finance.

Key Fact

Mumbai is home to about 22 million people in the metropolitan area and produces roughly 6% of India’s GDP from less than 0.1% of its land. Its harbour, airport and rail network drive its global role.

Mumbai’s Urban Structure

Mumbai has a recognisable land-use pattern. The southern tip houses the Central Business District (CBD) — Nariman Point and Fort — with skyscrapers, the stock exchange and headquarters of major banks. North of the CBD lies the inner city, including older industrial neighbourhoods and the famous slum of Dharavi — one of the largest slums in Asia, with around 700,000 residents on roughly 2 km². Beyond the inner city are suburbs such as Bandra and Andheri, which have been the focus of new high-rise apartment development. The urban-rural fringe includes the new airport at Navi Mumbai and growing satellite towns linked by motorway.

Population Growth

Mumbai’s population was about 1.5 million in 1941. By 1991 it had reached 12 million and by 2011 over 18 million. Two engines have driven growth. The first is natural increase — Mumbai has a young population so births greatly exceed deaths. The second is rural-urban migration. Migrants come from across India, especially from the poorer states of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra. Most are pushed by drought, debt and falling rural incomes; pulled by the chance of work in textiles, construction or domestic service. Around half of Mumbai’s residents now live in informal housing.

Mumbai offers genuine opportunities. Wages for unskilled work are roughly five times higher than in rural villages. Government schools and free public hospitals serve millions. Dharavi alone produces around US$1 billion of annual output from small-scale leather, pottery and recycling workshops; many residents are second-generation entrepreneurs, not destitute. The city has a vibrant cultural scene, top universities (IIT Bombay) and access to formal-sector jobs in finance and IT for those who can train into them.

Challenges of Rapid Growth

Growth has come at a cost. Mumbai faces severe housing shortages: an estimated 41% of residents live in slums. Property prices in the formal market are among the highest in the world — the same as central London — while incomes are far lower. Many slum residents have insecure property rights, meaning bulldozers can clear neighbourhoods with little notice. Public services struggle: clean water reaches some districts for only 2–4 hours a day, and large areas rely on shared public toilets. Traffic congestion costs the city an estimated 8% of GDP a year. Air pollution exceeds World Health Organization safe limits for most of the year, contributing to respiratory illness, especially in children.

Mumbai is one of the most unequal cities on Earth. Antilia, the home of the businessman Mukesh Ambani, is a 27-floor private skyscraper reportedly worth US$2 billion. It overlooks neighbourhoods where families pay 1,000 rupees a month (roughly £10) for a 10 m² tin-roofed shack. Two reasons explain the contrast: India’s rapid growth has rewarded skilled, English-speaking professionals far more than unskilled migrants; and the city’s land scarcity (built on a peninsula) has driven property prices to extreme levels, locking poorer residents out of formal housing. Politicians struggle to manage the gap because slum dwellers are also a powerful voting block.

Key Fact

Around 41% of Mumbai’s residents live in slums. Water reaches some districts only 2–4 hours per day. Traffic congestion costs the city about 8% of GDP a year. Air pollution exceeds WHO safe limits for most of the year.

before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark ‘Assess’ or ‘Examine’ questions, the strongest answers explicitly compare top-down with bottom-up. Use the structure: top-down example → strengths/weaknesses → bottom-up example → strengths/weaknesses → judgement. Examiners expect named projects (Mumbai Metro, SPARC toilets) not just ‘the government built things’. Conclude with a justified judgement — usually that both approaches are needed together.
